sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: CDC information relevant to herpesviral [herpes simplex] infections
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC explains herpes simplex infection, its clinical manifestations, sexual or oral exposure routes, and prevention measures.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports the ICD-10 B00 herpesviral [herpes simplex] infections category. Definition: herpes simplex virus type 1 and type 2 can cause oral or genital herpes infection. Clinical features: infection can cause painful sores, and some people have no symptoms. Epidemiology: genital herpes is a common sexually transmitted infection; burden and presentation vary by virus type and population. Transmission: infection can spread through contact with sores, saliva, genital fluids, or oral or genital skin, including when a partner has no visible sore. Prevention: avoiding sexual exposure, correct condom use, avoiding sex during symptoms, and clinician-directed suppressive antiviral treatment can reduce transmission risk.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: Herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 can cause oral or genital herpes; infection can cause painful sores or be asymptomatic.

content_sections.heading: Transmission and epidemiology
content_sections.text: Genital herpes is a common sexually transmitted infection and can spread through contact with infectious sores, saliva, genital fluids, or oral or genital skin.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Risk reduction includes avoiding exposure during symptoms, correct condom use, and clinician-directed suppressive antiviral treatment.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: CDC malaria clinical features, transmission, and prevention
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC identifies Plasmodium falciparum as a severe malaria species and describes clinical features, mosquito transmission, endemic settings, and prevention.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC malaria summary supports Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Definition: malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites, and P. falciparum infection can progress rapidly to severe or life-threatening disease. Clinical features: fever, chills, headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, anemia, neurologic manifestations, and severe organ complications can occur. Epidemiology: P. falciparum is common in many countries in sub-Saharan Africa and severe disease risk is greatest with substantial exposure in endemic settings. Transmission: most malaria follows bites from infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, with rare blood, organ, needle, or congenital transmission. Prevention: avoiding mosquito bites and taking indicated antimalarial prophylaxis are key travel-prevention measures.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: P. falciparum malaria can progress rapidly to severe disease with fever, anemia, neurologic manifestations, or organ complications.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: P. falciparum is common in many endemic settings, especially sub-Saharan Africa, and is mainly transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Mosquito-bite avoidance and indicated antimalarial prophylaxis reduce malaria risk.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: CDC malaria clinical features and transmission
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC malaria guidance describes P. malariae as a human malaria species, including clinical presentation, longer incubation, mosquito transmission, and prevention.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC malaria summary supports Plasmodium malariae malaria. Definition: malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites, including P. malariae. Clinical features: malaria may produce fever, chills, headache, malaise, nausea, anemia, jaundice, and in chronic or repeated P. malariae infection nephrotic syndrome can occur. Epidemiology: malaria risk occurs in endemic settings, and incubation periods are generally longer with P. malariae than with P. falciparum. Transmission: infection is mainly acquired from bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, with rare blood-borne or congenital routes. Prevention: mosquito-bite avoidance and indicated antimalarial prophylaxis are central prevention measures.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: P. malariae is a malaria parasite; malaria can cause febrile illness, anemia, and, with chronic or repeated P. malariae infection, nephrotic syndrome.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Risk occurs in malaria-endemic settings, incubation can be longer with P. malariae, and transmission is chiefly by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Avoiding mosquito bites and using indicated prophylaxis reduce malaria risk.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes VISA and VRSA as rare resistant S. aureus infections and addresses manifestations, healthcare-associated spread, infection prevention, and surveillance.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus infection (VISA). Definition: VISA is a type of antimicrobial-resistant S. aureus with reduced vancomycin susceptibility. Clinical features: infection can resemble other staphylococcal skin, wound, bloodstream, or other S. aureus infections. Epidemiology: vancomycin resistance in S. aureus is exceptionally rare and healthcare patients with devices, prior antibiotic exposure, or underlying conditions are at increased risk. Transmission: resistant S. aureus can spread through close physical contact or contaminated wound material, particularly in healthcare settings. Prevention: hand hygiene, avoiding contact with wounds or contaminated material, and recommended healthcare infection-control precautions reduce spread.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: VISA is antimicrobial-resistant S. aureus with reduced vancomycin susceptibility and can cause staphylococcal infections including skin or wound infection.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: VISA is rare; healthcare exposure, invasive devices, antibiotic exposure, and contact with contaminated wound material are relevant risk or spread contexts.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Hand hygiene and healthcare infection-control precautions reduce spread.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes VRSA and VISA as rare resistant S. aureus infections and addresses manifestations, healthcare-associated spread, infection prevention, and surveillance.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection (VRSA). Definition: VRSA is a type of antimicrobial-resistant S. aureus that is resistant to vancomycin. Clinical features: infection can present as skin, wound, or other staphylococcal infection. Epidemiology: VRSA infections are exceptionally rare and risk is concentrated among people with relevant healthcare exposure, invasive devices, underlying conditions, or prior antibiotic exposure. Transmission: VRSA could spread through close physical contact or contaminated material in ways similar to other resistant S. aureus. Prevention: hand hygiene, avoiding contact with wounds or contaminated material, and recommended hospital precautions reduce spread.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: VRSA is vancomycin-resistant S. aureus and can cause skin, wound, or other staphylococcal infection.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: VRSA is exceptionally rare; healthcare exposure and contact with contaminated wound material are relevant contexts.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Hand hygiene and healthcare infection-control precautions reduce spread.

aliases: Australian flavivirus infection unspecified case definition

sources.source_name: Australian Government Department of Health and Aged Care
sources.title: Flavivirus infection (unspecified) including Zika virus - surveillance case definition
sources.raw_excerpt: The Australian national surveillance definition uses flavivirus infection (unspecified) when a human flavivirus infection cannot be assigned to one specific virus and specifies the notification and laboratory-clinical classification boundary.
sources.content_text: This reviewed Australian Government summary supports the surveillance concept Flavivirus infection (unspecified). Definition: the category is used for a human flavivirus infection that cannot be attributed to a single known flavivirus because available laboratory results are non-specific, cannot identify the virus, or identify a flavivirus not otherwise classified. Surveillance and reporting: the national definition requires the stated laboratory and clinical evidence for a confirmed notification and retains separate handling for Zika virus classifications. Clinical context: the definition describes non-encephalitic febrile illness and encephalitic illness as compatible clinical presentations. Interpretation: this is a surveillance category with a laboratory-classification boundary, not a claim that all flavivirus infections have the same clinical course or prevention measures.

content_sections.heading: Definition and classification boundary
content_sections.text: Flavivirus infection (unspecified) is an Australian surveillance category for human infection that cannot be assigned to one specific flavivirus because available testing is non-specific, cannot identify the virus, or identifies a flavivirus not otherwise classified.

content_sections.heading: Notification and clinical context
content_sections.text: The national definition specifies laboratory and clinical evidence for confirmed notification and describes compatible febrile or encephalitic clinical presentations.

content_sections.heading: Surveillance interpretation
content_sections.text: The category is a reporting and laboratory-classification boundary; trend interpretation should preserve the current case-definition scope and distinct Zika virus handling.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About Chlamydia pneumoniae infection
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes C. pneumoniae respiratory infection, including symptoms, occurrence, droplet transmission, and hygiene-based prevention.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports chlamydial pneumonia caused by Chlamydia pneumoniae. Definition: C. pneumoniae is a bacterium that can infect the upper or lower respiratory tract and cause bronchitis or pneumonia. Clinical features: fatigue, headache, hoarseness, low-grade fever, runny nose, sore throat, and slowly worsening cough are common; serious complications are uncommon. Epidemiology: first infection commonly occurs in school-aged children or young adults, while reinfection and severe disease are more common in older adults and outbreaks can occur in crowded settings. Transmission: people spread the bacteria by coughing or sneezing respiratory droplets, and contaminated droplets can reach the mouth or nose. Prevention: covering coughs and sneezes and regular hand hygiene help reduce spread; no vaccine is available.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: C. pneumoniae can cause upper or lower respiratory infection, bronchitis, or pneumonia with cough, fever, or other respiratory symptoms.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Infection often begins in school-aged children or young adults; respiratory droplets and contaminated hands or surfaces can spread bacteria.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Cough etiquette and hand hygiene help reduce spread; no vaccine is available.

sources.source_name: NIH MedlinePlus
sources.title: Roseola medical encyclopedia
sources.raw_excerpt: MedlinePlus describes roseola as a viral infection in young children and notes its symptoms and hand-hygiene prevention advice.
sources.content_text: This reviewed NIH MedlinePlus summary supports roseola, also called exanthem subitum or sixth disease. Definition: roseola is a viral infection that commonly affects infants and young children. Clinical features: illness typically includes several days of high fever followed by a rash as the fever resolves; febrile seizures can occur. Epidemiology: roseola is a common childhood infection, especially in infants and young children. Transmission: human herpesviruses associated with roseola spread between close contacts, including through saliva or respiratory secretions. Prevention: careful handwashing helps reduce spread of viruses that cause roseola.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: Roseola is a viral illness of infants and young children marked by high fever followed by a rash; febrile seizures can occur.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Roseola is common in early childhood and associated viruses can spread among close contacts through saliva or respiratory secretions.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Careful handwashing helps reduce spread.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About B virus
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes B virus as a rare, potentially fatal macaque-associated infection and provides clinical, exposure, prevention, and first-aid information.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports herpes B virus infection. Definition: B virus is a macaque-associated alphaherpesvirus that can cause rare but severe infection in people. Clinical features: early fever and chills can progress to local blisters, neurologic disease, respiratory compromise, or death. Epidemiology: risk is very low for the general public but greater for people who work with or are exposed to macaques. Transmission: infection can follow macaque bites or scratches, contact of infected tissue or fluid with broken skin or mucosa, contaminated sharps, or relevant animal-facility exposure. Prevention: avoid contact with macaques, follow laboratory and animal-facility protocols, and immediately wash exposed skin and obtain medical assessment after a possible exposure.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: B virus is a rare macaque-associated infection that can progress from febrile illness to severe neurologic or respiratory disease.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Risk is concentrated in people exposed to macaques; bites, scratches, infected fluids, and contaminated sharps can transmit infection.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Avoid macaque contact, use appropriate facility protocols, and immediately wash and seek care after exposure.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About Non-Polio Enteroviruses
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes non-polio enterovirus infections, including serious complications, routes of spread, seasonal occurrence, and hygiene-based prevention.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports the enterovirus infection with severe complications surveillance concept. Definition: non-polio enteroviruses are common viruses that can cause mild illness or serious complications. Clinical features: fever, respiratory symptoms, rash, mouth blisters, and muscle aches can occur; complications can include viral meningitis, encephalitis, myocarditis, pericarditis, acute flaccid paralysis, or severe neonatal sepsis. Epidemiology: CDC estimates 10 to 15 million non-polio enterovirus infections and tens of thousands of hospitalizations annually in the United States; infections are common in summer and fall, and infants, children, and immunocompromised people have greater complication risk. Transmission: virus can spread for weeks through respiratory or oral secretions, blister fluid, stool, close contact, contaminated surfaces, diaper changing, or contaminated drinking water. Prevention: wash hands with soap and water, clean and disinfect shared surfaces, avoid close contact with infected people, and note that no vaccine protects against non-polio enterovirus infection.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: Non-polio enteroviruses can cause mild illness or serious complications including meningitis, encephalitis, myocarditis, paralysis, or severe neonatal sepsis.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: CDC estimates 10 to 15 million U.S. infections annually, often in summer and fall; virus can spread through respiratory or oral secretions, blister fluid, stool, close contact, contaminated surfaces, diaper changing, or contaminated water.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Handwashing with soap and water, cleaning and disinfection, and avoiding close contact reduce spread; no vaccine protects against non-polio enterovirus infection.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: CDC clinical presentation of COVID-19
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes severe COVID-19 risk, clinical presentation, SARS-CoV-2 transmission, and vaccine-based prevention.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports the severe complicated COVID-19 surveillance concept. Definition: COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, and severe illness is a serious clinical presentation requiring prompt assessment. Clinical features: severe disease can include lower respiratory involvement, hypoxemia, respiratory distress, or need for hospitalization. Epidemiology: older age, immunocompromise, and certain underlying conditions increase the risk of severe outcomes. Transmission: people with SARS-CoV-2 infection can transmit virus before symptoms, with symptoms, or without symptoms, chiefly through respiratory particles in close or poorly ventilated settings. Prevention: staying up to date with COVID-19 vaccination and following respiratory-virus guidance reduce risks of infection, hospitalization, and death.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: Severe COVID-19 is a serious SARS-CoV-2 clinical presentation that can involve lower respiratory disease, hypoxemia, or hospitalization.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Older age, immunocompromise, and underlying conditions increase severe-outcome risk; SARS-CoV-2 can spread through respiratory particles from symptomatic or asymptomatic people.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Vaccination and respiratory-virus precautions reduce infection and severe-outcome risk.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Hepatitis C basics
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes chronic hepatitis C, its often limited symptoms, blood-borne transmission, prevention, and testing.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports chronic hepatitis C. Definition: hepatitis C is infection with hepatitis C virus, and more than half of infections become chronic. Clinical features: chronic infection is often asymptomatic or associated with nonspecific fatigue or depression, but untreated infection can cause liver disease, liver failure, or liver cancer. Epidemiology: chronic hepatitis C is a public-health concern because many infected people do not know they are infected. Transmission: HCV spreads when infected blood enters another person's body, particularly through sharing contaminated injection equipment; childbirth and some other blood exposures are less common routes. Prevention: there is no vaccine, so prevention emphasizes avoiding blood exposure, not sharing needles or items contaminated with blood, and recommended testing and treatment.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: More than half of hepatitis C infections become chronic; many people have no symptoms, but untreated infection can lead to severe liver disease.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Many infected people are unaware of infection; HCV is chiefly transmitted through blood exposure, especially shared injection equipment.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: There is no vaccine; avoiding blood exposure, testing, and treatment are central prevention measures.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: CDC recommendations for perinatally exposed infants and children
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC provides evidence and testing recommendations for infants and children exposed to hepatitis C virus during pregnancy or childbirth.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports perinatal hepatitis C. Definition: perinatal HCV infection concerns infants or children exposed to hepatitis C virus during pregnancy or childbirth. Clinical features: infection may not be apparent in infancy, so recommended testing is important to identify children with infection and guide care. Epidemiology: maternal detectable HCV RNA is a known risk factor for perinatal transmission, and public-health recommendations address testing of exposed children. Transmission: HCV can be transmitted from a pregnant person with viremic infection to an infant around birth; delivery and exposure factors can influence risk. Prevention: hepatitis C testing during pregnancy, appropriate pregnancy and delivery management, and timely testing of perinatally exposed infants support prevention of missed infection and later complications.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: Perinatal hepatitis C concerns infant exposure around pregnancy or childbirth and can require testing because infection may not be clinically apparent.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Maternal detectable HCV RNA is a known risk factor, and transmission can occur from a viremic pregnant person around birth.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Pregnancy testing, appropriate care, and timely testing of exposed infants support prevention and early identification.

aliases: Severe invasive group A streptococcal infection

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Clinical considerations for group A Streptococcus
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes invasive group A streptococcal disease, serious manifestations, transmission, prevention, and surveillance.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports severe invasive streptococcal infection. Definition: group A Streptococcus can cause invasive disease when bacteria affect normally sterile body sites. Clinical features: invasive disease includes severe cellulitis with bloodstream infection, pneumonia, necrotizing fasciitis, and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. Epidemiology: CDC tracks invasive group A streptococcal disease, and rates are highest in older adults with documented outbreaks in healthcare and long-term-care settings. Transmission: group A strep most often spreads person to person through respiratory droplets or contact with secretions, with healthcare-associated spread documented. Prevention: limiting exposure, prompt diagnosis and treatment, appropriate infection-control precautions, and targeted prophylaxis in selected situations help prevent spread; no vaccine is currently available.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: Invasive group A strep affects normally sterile sites and can include pneumonia, necrotizing fasciitis, or streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: CDC tracks invasive disease; older adults and healthcare or long-term-care settings are important occurrence contexts, and respiratory droplets or secretions can spread bacteria.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Prompt diagnosis, treatment, infection-control precautions, and selected prophylaxis support prevention; no vaccine is available.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About Pseudomonas aeruginosa
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa, healthcare-associated infection, transmission contexts, and infection prevention.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection. Definition: P. aeruginosa is an environmental bacterium that can cause human infection, and multidrug-resistant forms are difficult to treat because of resistance to many antibiotics. Clinical features: infections can affect the bloodstream, lungs, urinary tract, wounds, or surgical sites. Epidemiology: infections typically occur in healthcare settings; patients using ventilators or catheters and people with surgical wounds or burns are at elevated risk. Transmission: exposure can involve contaminated surfaces, equipment, soil or water, or contaminated hands. Prevention: hand hygiene, core infection-prevention and control practices, environmental cleaning, and healthcare water-management measures reduce risk.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: MDR P. aeruginosa is a difficult-to-treat resistant form that can cause bloodstream, lung, urinary, wound, or surgical-site infection.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Healthcare patients with devices, wounds, or burns are at elevated risk; contaminated equipment, surfaces, water, soil, or hands can be exposure routes.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Hand hygiene, infection-control practices, environmental cleaning, and water management reduce risk.

aliases: Infectious syphilis less than two years duration
Primary secondary and early latent syphilis Australia

sources.source_name: Australian Government Department of Health and Aged Care
sources.title: Syphilis (less than 2 years duration) – surveillance case definition
sources.raw_excerpt: The Australian national surveillance case definition treats infectious syphilis of less than two years duration as a notifiable category that includes primary, secondary and early latent infection and specifies confirmed and probable case criteria.
sources.content_text: This reviewed summary reflects the Australian national surveillance case-definition document for infectious syphilis of less than two years duration. The category includes primary, secondary and early latent syphilis and is used by state and territory health departments when deciding whether a case should be notified nationally. Confirmed classification can be based on definitive laboratory evidence, or on suggestive laboratory evidence together with compatible clinical evidence. The laboratory pathways include recent seroconversion, a substantial rise in non-treponemal antibody titre with treponemal confirmation, direct demonstration of Treponema pallidum, or specified combinations of treponemal and non-treponemal tests. Compatible clinical evidence includes a primary chancre or signs of secondary syphilis. The definition also describes probable cases using laboratory findings together with treatment history, contact, immunoglobulin M, or titre criteria. The less-than-two-year boundary is a surveillance classification and must not be interpreted as a claim that every infection date is known exactly. Both confirmed and probable cases meeting the national definition are reportable, and trend interpretation should retain the applicable definition version and jurisdictional notification practice.

content_sections.heading: Definition and reporting
content_sections.text: The nationally notifiable category covers infectious syphilis of less than two years duration, including primary, secondary and early latent infection. Confirmed and probable cases meeting the surveillance definition are notified.

content_sections.heading: Clinical and laboratory scope
content_sections.text: Classification combines specified laboratory evidence with clinical findings such as a primary chancre or signs of secondary syphilis; recent seroconversion and qualifying antibody-titre changes are among the laboratory pathways.

content_sections.heading: Surveillance interpretation
content_sections.text: The duration boundary is a national reporting classification. Comparisons should preserve the definition version, confirmed-versus-probable scope, and jurisdictional notification practice.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About syphilis
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes syphilis stages, clinical manifestations, sexual and congenital transmission, and prevention.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supplements the Australian less-than-two-years surveillance definition for infectious syphilis. Definition: syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection that progresses through primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary stages; primary, secondary, and early latent infection make up the infectious early-duration context. Clinical features: stages have different manifestations, including sores in primary infection and other signs in secondary infection. Epidemiology: syphilis is a common sexually transmitted infection, and surveillance interpretation should retain the Australian less-than-two-years duration definition. Transmission: infection spreads through sexual contact with infectious lesions and can also pass during pregnancy. Prevention: reducing sexual exposure risk, correct condom use, testing, and timely treatment help prevent transmission.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: The Australian early-duration surveillance category includes primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis; stages have different clinical manifestations.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Syphilis is a common sexually transmitted infection; it spreads through sexual contact with infectious lesions and can pass during pregnancy.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Testing, timely treatment, risk reduction, and correct condom use help prevent transmission.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Food poisoning from marine toxins
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC identifies paralytic shellfish poisoning as a severe foodborne toxin syndrome caused by saxitoxin-contaminated shellfish and describes worldwide occurrence and clinical manifestations.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC Yellow Book summary supports paralytic shellfish poisoning. Definition: paralytic shellfish poisoning is a foodborne marine-toxin syndrome caused by eating shellfish contaminated with saxitoxins produced by dinoflagellates. Clinical features: symptoms can include gastrointestinal, neurologic, cardiovascular, or respiratory effects, with severe cases causing ataxia, paralysis, respiratory failure, or death. Epidemiology: PSP occurs worldwide and is especially reported in temperate waters off Atlantic and Pacific North America, including Alaska, with cases also reported in the Americas, Asia, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand. Exposure and prevention context: illness follows contaminated shellfish consumption, so monitoring shellfish harvesting areas and avoiding unsafe or unregulated shellfish are central public-health controls.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: PSP follows consumption of saxitoxin-contaminated shellfish and can cause gastrointestinal, neurologic, cardiovascular, or respiratory illness including paralysis.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology
content_sections.text: PSP occurs worldwide, including temperate waters of North America and reported regions in the Americas, Asia, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand.

content_sections.heading: Exposure and prevention context
content_sections.text: Public-health control relies on shellfish monitoring and avoiding unsafe or unregulated shellfish consumption.

aliases: Primary secondary and early latent syphilis

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About syphilis
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes syphilis stages, manifestations, sexual and congenital transmission, and prevention.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports infectious syphilis, including primary, secondary, and early latent stages. Definition: syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary stages; early stages are the infectious clinical context. Clinical features: primary disease can cause one or more sores, while secondary disease can have different systemic or mucocutaneous signs; stage-specific symptoms vary. Epidemiology: syphilis is a common sexually transmitted infection and observed notification patterns depend on screening and surveillance definitions. Transmission: infection spreads through sexual contact with infectious lesions and can pass from a pregnant person to a fetus. Prevention: testing, timely treatment, reducing sexual exposure risk, and correct condom use help prevent transmission, though lesions outside condom coverage can still transmit infection.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: Infectious syphilis includes early-stage primary, secondary, and early latent infection, with stage-specific sores and other manifestations.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Syphilis is a common sexually transmitted infection that spreads through contact with infectious lesions and can pass during pregnancy.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Testing, prompt treatment, risk reduction, and correct condom use help prevent transmission.

aliases: Syphilis more than two years or unknown duration
Syphilis greater than 2 years or unspecified duration

sources.source_name: Australian Government Department of Health and Aged Care
sources.title: Australia's notifiable diseases status, 2005 – sexually transmissible diseases
sources.raw_excerpt: The official NNDSS annual report distinguishes infectious syphilis of less than two years duration from syphilis of more than two years or unknown duration and describes the latter surveillance category and its confirmed-case boundary.
sources.content_text: This reviewed summary reflects the Australian Government NNDSS annual-report section on sexually transmissible diseases. Adult syphilis notifications were reported in two separate duration categories: infectious syphilis of less than two years duration, and syphilis of more than two years or unknown duration. The second category is a combined surveillance bucket rather than a distinct organism or transmission route. Its confirmed-case definition applies when the case does not meet the less-than-two-year category and has qualifying reactive treponemal serology confirmed by a reactive non-treponemal test or another treponemal test, together with no documented history of adequate previous treatment or endemic treponemal disease under the stated definition. The annual report presents notifications and rates separately for the two categories and notes that screening and reporting practice can affect observed patterns. Counts in the more-than-two-years-or-unknown category therefore combine infections with different or uncertain timing and must not be interpreted as incident infectious syphilis. Trend comparisons should preserve the Australian category label, definition period, and confirmed-case reporting basis, and the two duration categories should not be merged without an explicit analytic reason.

content_sections.heading: Classification definition
content_sections.text: Australian NNDSS reporting separates adult syphilis into less-than-two-years infectious syphilis and a combined more-than-two-years-or-unknown-duration category. The latter is a reporting bucket, not a separate pathogen.

content_sections.heading: Included conditions and laboratory boundary
content_sections.text: The category includes confirmed syphilis that does not meet the less-than-two-year definition and satisfies the stated serologic and treatment-history criteria; infection timing may be older or unknown.

content_sections.heading: Monitoring interpretation
content_sections.text: Notifications and rates are reported separately by duration category. Screening, classification, and reporting practices affect trends, so the category must not be treated as incident infectious syphilis.

aliases: E. coli enteritis all reported pathotypes

sources.source_name: Norwegian Institute of Public Health (FHI)
sources.title: E. coli enteritis excluding EHEC infection and HUS – handbook for health professionals
sources.raw_excerpt: FHI describes diarrheagenic E. coli groups including EIEC, EPEC, ETEC and EAEC, their epidemiology, and their reporting history in Norway, while directing EHEC and HUS to a separate chapter.
sources.content_text: This reviewed summary reflects the Norwegian Institute of Public Health handbook page for E. coli enteritis other than EHEC infection and haemolytic uraemic syndrome. FHI explains that most Escherichia coli are harmless intestinal flora but several diarrheagenic groups can cause enteric infection. The non-EHEC reporting scope includes enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC), enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC, including typical and atypical forms), enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC), and enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC). The page explicitly directs EHEC infection and HUS to a separate chapter, making the boundary between these surveillance components clear. It describes human reservoirs for several pathotypes, animal reservoirs for some forms, and food, water, environmental, or person-to-person exposure contexts. E. coli enteritis was historically reportable for children during an earlier period, and all cases have been notifiable to MSIS since 1989 under the described scope. FHI notes that observed increases for some pathotypes are affected by expanded use of sensitive multiplex PCR and broader testing. Counts can also include PCR findings that do not fully distinguish EIEC from Shigella, so longitudinal interpretation must preserve diagnostic method and pathotype definitions.

content_sections.heading: Included non-EHEC pathotypes
content_sections.text: The FHI non-EHEC chapter covers EIEC, typical and atypical EPEC, ETEC and EAEC. EHEC infection and HUS are handled separately.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and exposure
content_sections.text: Reservoirs and exposure routes differ by pathotype and can involve humans, animals, food, water, environments or person-to-person spread.

content_sections.heading: MSIS interpretation
content_sections.text: All cases have been notifiable since 1989. Changes in PCR testing intensity and the inability of some assays to separate EIEC from Shigella affect reported trends.

sources.source_name: Norwegian Institute of Public Health (FHI)
sources.title: EHEC infection and HUS – handbook for health professionals
sources.raw_excerpt: FHI describes enterohaemorrhagic or Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli as the EHEC/STEC component of Norwegian E. coli enteritis surveillance and explains severity, reservoirs, reporting and diagnostic changes.
sources.content_text: This reviewed summary reflects the Norwegian Institute of Public Health handbook page for enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli infection and haemolytic uraemic syndrome. FHI uses EHEC for the established Norwegian surveillance label while noting the international shift toward the broader term Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli (STEC). EHEC or STEC can range from asymptomatic infection to severe bloody diarrhoea and may cause haemolytic uraemic syndrome. Virulence classification uses Shiga-toxin genes and subtypes together with other bacterial and host factors. Ruminants are an important reservoir, and exposure can involve food, water, animals, environments, or person-to-person transmission. E. coli enteritis including EHEC has been notifiable to MSIS since 1989, while diarrhoea-associated HUS became separately notifiable later. FHI describes changes in primary-laboratory testing and broader examination of stool samples as important influences on observed notification trends. High-virulence or suspected high-virulence findings receive additional follow-up and isolate verification. This EHEC/STEC component is distinct from the non-EHEC pathotypes described on the companion FHI page, but both components may appear in a source-reported all-pathotype E. coli enteritis aggregate.

content_sections.heading: EHEC and STEC component
content_sections.text: FHI retains EHEC as the Norwegian surveillance label and relates it to STEC. Infection ranges from asymptomatic carriage to bloody diarrhoea and HUS.

content_sections.heading: Exposure and severity
content_sections.text: Ruminants are an important reservoir; food, water, animal, environmental and person-to-person exposures occur. Shiga-toxin profiles and host factors influence severity.

content_sections.heading: Reporting boundary
content_sections.text: E. coli enteritis including EHEC has been notifiable to MSIS since 1989, and diagnostic expansion affects trends. EHEC/STEC is a distinct component from other diarrheagenic pathotypes.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Clinical Overview of Haemophilus influenzae Disease
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes H. influenzae disease, including respiratory-droplet transmission, the possibility of neonatal exposure, and prevention measures for Hib disease.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports Haemophilus influenzae disease. Transmission: people with symptomatic infection and nasopharyngeal carriage can spread H. influenzae through respiratory droplets generated by coughing or sneezing; newborn infection can follow aspiration of infected amniotic fluid or contact with infected genital-tract secretions. Prevention: CDC recommends Hib chemoprophylaxis for specified close contacts and advises clinicians to follow current prevention guidance.

content_sections.heading: Transmission
content_sections.text: Haemophilus influenzae transmission usually occurs when a person breathes in or directly contacts respiratory droplets containing the bacteria. Symptomatic people and nasopharyngeal carriers can spread bacteria by coughing or sneezing; newborn exposure can occur around delivery.

content_sections.heading: Prevention context
content_sections.text: CDC recommends chemoprophylaxis for specified close contacts of Hib cases and directs clinicians to current prevention guidance.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Preventing Parvovirus B19
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC explains how parvovirus B19 spreads, its seasonal and outbreak pattern, and respiratory-virus prevention measures.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), a manifestation of parvovirus B19 infection. Epidemiology: in the United States, parvovirus B19 infection occurs more often in late winter, spring, and early summer, and minor outbreaks occur about every three to four years. Transmission: parvovirus B19 spreads from person to person through respiratory particles, can spread through blood or blood products, and can pass during pregnancy from mother to baby. Prevention: there is no vaccine to prevent parvovirus B19 infection; good hygiene, cleaner air, and actions to prevent respiratory-virus spread reduce transmission risk.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology
content_sections.text: In the United States, parvovirus B19 infection occurs more often in late winter, spring, and early summer. Minor outbreaks occur about every three to four years.

content_sections.heading: Transmission
content_sections.text: Parvovirus B19 can spread person to person through respiratory particles, through blood or blood products, and during pregnancy from mother to baby.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: There is no vaccine to prevent parvovirus B19 infection. Good hygiene, cleaner air, and actions to prevent respiratory-virus spread help reduce transmission risk.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Classic Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC explains that most classic CJD is sporadic, while rare iatrogenic cases have been linked to healthcare or biological-product exposure and have declined after decontamination-procedure changes.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports classic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). Prevention: classic CJD is most often sporadic, but rare iatrogenic cases have followed exposure to prions in healthcare settings or biological products. CDC reports that cases linked to contaminated surgical or medical equipment have not been reported since changes in equipment decontamination procedures; prevention therefore depends on appropriate prion-control procedures for relevant instruments and tissues.

content_sections.heading: Prevention of iatrogenic transmission
content_sections.text: Rare iatrogenic CJD has followed contact with prions in healthcare settings or biological products. CDC reports no known cases from contaminated surgical or medical equipment since procedure changes to decontaminate equipment, supporting prion-control prevention for relevant instruments and tissues.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Reducing Risk for Cryptococcosis
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes Cryptococcus exposure, the higher risk among people with weakened immunity, and targeted screening that can prevent severe cryptococcosis in people with HIV.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports disseminated cryptococcosis. Prevention: Cryptococcus is difficult to avoid in the environment and CDC gives no formal general recommendation to prevent infection. For people with advanced HIV, targeted cryptococcal-antigen screening followed by antifungal treatment when indicated can prevent severe or life-threatening cryptococcosis.

content_sections.heading: Prevention and targeted screening
content_sections.text: CDC has no formal general recommendation to prevent cryptococcal infection because exposure in the environment is difficult to avoid. Targeted cryptococcal-antigen screening in people with advanced HIV, with treatment when antigen is detected, can prevent severe cryptococcosis.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Clinical Considerations for Group A Streptococcus
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes group A streptococcal transmission through droplets or secretions and prevention through limiting exposure, treatment, infection control, and selected prophylaxis.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports invasive group A streptococcal infection. Transmission: group A Streptococcus most often spreads directly person to person through respiratory droplets and can also spread through contact with infected saliva, wound drainage, or nasal secretions. Prevention: prevention activities include limiting exposure and spread, treating group A streptococcal infections, applying infection-control precautions, and using preventive antibiotics when appropriate; no vaccine is currently available.

content_sections.heading: Transmission
content_sections.text: Group A Streptococcus is most often transmitted directly person to person through respiratory droplets. Contact with infected saliva, wound drainage, or nasal secretions can also spread bacteria.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: Prevention includes limiting exposure and spread, prompt treatment, appropriate infection-control precautions, and preventive antibiotics when appropriate. No vaccine is currently available.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Rickettsial Diseases - CDC Yellow Book
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes arthropod transmission of rickettsial diseases and prevention approaches for travelers at risk of vector exposure.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC Yellow Book summary supports rickettsial diseases. Prevention: prevention focuses on avoiding bites and contact with arthropod vectors such as ticks, fleas, lice, and mites, using the vector-specific protective measures described for travel and exposure settings.

content_sections.heading: Prevention of vector exposure
content_sections.text: Rickettsial disease prevention focuses on avoiding exposure to arthropod vectors, including ticks, fleas, lice, and mites, with protective measures appropriate to the travel or exposure setting.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Clinical Overview of Chickenpox (Varicella)
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes the epidemiologic impact of varicella vaccination and identifies complication patterns that can require clinical care.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports complicated varicella. Epidemiology: routine varicella vaccination has substantially reduced varicella illness, hospitalizations, and deaths in the United States, but infections and complications still occur. Complication patterns differ by age, with bacterial skin and soft-tissue infection common among affected children and pneumonia common among affected adults.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and complication patterns
content_sections.text: Varicella vaccination has substantially reduced illness, hospitalizations, and deaths in the United States, although infections and complications continue to occur. Bacterial skin and soft-tissue infection is a common complication in children and pneumonia is common in adults.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About Influenza
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes influenza as a contagious respiratory illness, including droplet transmission and the less common role of contaminated surfaces.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports severe complicated influenza. Transmission: influenza viruses mainly spread through droplets made when a person with influenza coughs, sneezes, or talks; less often, a person can become infected after touching a contaminated surface or object and then touching the mouth, nose, or eyes.

content_sections.heading: Transmission
content_sections.text: Influenza viruses mainly spread through respiratory droplets produced when people cough, sneeze, or talk. Less commonly, contaminated surfaces or objects can contribute to exposure when people touch their mouth, nose, or eyes.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About Epidemic Typhus
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC defines epidemic typhus as louse-borne Rickettsia prowazekii infection, describes its crowding-associated occurrence, and provides prevention information.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC summary supports epidemic typhus fever. Definition: epidemic typhus, also called louse-borne typhus, is an uncommon infection caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii. Epidemiology: it is now rare but can occur where extreme overcrowding allows body lice to move from person to person; rare United States cases can follow exposure to flying squirrels and their nests. Transmission: people acquire infection through contact with infected body lice. Prevention: no vaccine is available; preventing and controlling body-lice infestation, including access to bathing and clean clothes, reduces risk.

content_sections.heading: Definition and epidemiology
content_sections.text: Epidemic typhus, also called louse-borne typhus, is an uncommon Rickettsia prowazekii infection. It is now rare but can occur in overcrowded settings where body lice move between people; rare United States cases have followed flying-squirrel exposure.

content_sections.heading: Transmission
content_sections.text: Epidemic typhus is transmitted through contact with infected body lice.

content_sections.heading: Prevention
content_sections.text: No vaccine is available for epidemic typhus. Prevention focuses on controlling body lice and improving access to bathing and clean clothing.

aliases: Occupational blood and body fluid exposure

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, NIOSH
sources.title: Bloodborne Infectious Disease Risk Factors for Healthcare Workers
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC/NIOSH defines occupational blood and body-fluid exposure routes, identifies healthcare workers at risk, and describes immediate reporting, post-exposure care, and prevention measures.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC/NIOSH summary supports a work accident with biological material, an occupational exposure concept. Definition: a work accident with biological material can involve a needlestick puncture, another sharps injury, or contact of blood or potentially infectious body fluids with a worker. Clinical assessment: the exposure can place a worker at risk of bloodborne infection, including hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or HIV, and requires prompt occupational-health evaluation rather than being a single disease with fixed symptoms. Epidemiology: healthcare workers are an at-risk occupational population because blood and body-fluid exposures occur in clinical work settings. Transmission: bloodborne pathogens can be transmitted after a needlestick, sharps injury, or contact with patient blood or other body fluids. Prevention: Standard Precautions, safer devices, personal protective equipment, immediate washing and reporting of an exposure, risk assessment, and indicated post-exposure prophylaxis reduce occupational infection risk.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical assessment
content_sections.text: A work accident with biological material includes a needlestick puncture, another sharps injury, or contact with blood or potentially infectious body fluids. It can place a worker at risk of bloodborne infection and requires prompt occupational-health evaluation.

content_sections.heading: Occupational epidemiology and transmission
content_sections.text: Healthcare workers are an at-risk occupational population for blood and body-fluid exposure. Bloodborne pathogens can be transmitted after a needlestick, another sharps injury, or contact with patient blood or other body fluids.

content_sections.heading: Prevention and response
content_sections.text: Standard Precautions, safer devices, personal protective equipment, immediate washing and reporting, risk assessment, and indicated post-exposure prophylaxis reduce occupational infection risk.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV) - STI Treatment Guidelines
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes LGV diagnosis and management, including treatment, follow-up, sex-partner evaluation and treatment, and measures that prevent ongoing transmission or tissue damage.
sources.content_text: This reviewed CDC STI Treatment Guidelines summary supports lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV). Definition: LGV is a sexually transmitted infection caused by invasive L1, L2, or L3 strains of Chlamydia trachomatis. Clinical context: LGV can present with genital or colorectal disease and lymphadenopathy or proctocolitis syndromes. Prevention: prompt evaluation, recommended treatment, follow-up testing, and evaluation and presumptive treatment of recent sex partners help prevent ongoing transmission and complications; patients are advised to avoid sex until treatment is complete and symptoms have resolved. Surveillance context: LGV diagnosis should also prompt testing for other sexually transmitted infections according to the guidance.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical context
content_sections.text: LGV is a sexually transmitted infection caused by invasive L1, L2, or L3 strains of Chlamydia trachomatis and can present with genital or colorectal syndromes and lymphadenopathy.

content_sections.heading: Prevention and partner management
content_sections.text: Prompt recommended treatment, follow-up testing, evaluation and presumptive treatment of recent sex partners, and avoiding sex until treatment is complete and symptoms resolve help prevent ongoing transmission and complications.

content_sections.heading: Associated STI testing
content_sections.text: CDC guidance recommends testing people diagnosed with LGV for other sexually transmitted infections, with follow-up after treatment.

sources.source_name: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About Cronobacter Infection
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC describes Cronobacter infection as a rare but potentially life-threatening infection in infants, including its exposure routes, clinical manifestations, prevention, and reporting context.
sources.content_text: This reviewed summary reflects the CDC overview of Cronobacter infection. Cronobacter sakazakii and related species are environmental bacteria that can contaminate dry foods, especially powdered infant formula, and infant feeding items. Infection is rare but may be severe in newborns and young infants. In infants, early symptoms can include fever, poor feeding, excessive crying, very low energy, or seizures; serious outcomes include bloodstream infection, meningitis, urinary tract infection, and wound infection. Exposure can occur when powdered formula, water, feeding items, or preparation surfaces are contaminated. CDC identifies safe preparation and storage of formula, hand and surface hygiene, and cleaning and sanitizing feeding items as prevention measures. CDC notes that historic reporting coverage limited incidence estimates in the United States, while invasive infant infection became nationally notifiable in 2024.

content_sections.heading: Definition and epidemiology
content_sections.text: Cronobacter are environmental bacteria that can contaminate powdered infant formula and feeding items. Infection is rare, disproportionately severe in newborns and young infants, and historical reporting coverage limited United States incidence estimates before invasive infant infection became nationally notifiable in 2024.

content_sections.heading: Clinical features and transmission
content_sections.text: Infants may develop fever, poor feeding, excessive crying, low energy, or seizures. Severe disease can include sepsis or meningitis. Exposure can follow contamination of powdered formula, water, feeding items, or preparation surfaces.

content_sections.heading: Prevention and surveillance
content_sections.text: CDC prevention guidance emphasizes safe formula preparation and storage, hand and surface hygiene, and cleaning and sanitizing feeding items. Invasive infant infection is a nationally notifiable condition in the United States.

sources.source_name: Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare
sources.title: Japanese spotted fever notification criteria
sources.raw_excerpt: Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare defines Japanese spotted fever, describes infection through hard-tick bites and clinical characteristics, and specifies notification criteria.
sources.content_text: This reviewed summary reflects the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare notification page for Japanese spotted fever. The condition is infection caused by Rickettsia japonica. It is acquired through bites from infected hard ticks. Illness can begin about two to eight days after a bite with headache, malaise, high fever, and a red maculopapular rash that can begin on the extremities; the page also notes laboratory abnormalities and potential severe progression. Physicians are required to notify cases meeting the clinical and laboratory criteria under the Infectious Diseases Control Law.

content_sections.heading: Definition, clinical features, and transmission
content_sections.text: Japanese spotted fever is infection caused by Rickettsia japonica and is acquired through bites from infected hard ticks. Symptoms can include headache, malaise, high fever, and a maculopapular rash; severe progression can occur.

content_sections.heading: Surveillance
content_sections.text: Physicians notify cases meeting the specified clinical and laboratory criteria under Japan's Infectious Diseases Control Law.

sources.source_name: Japan National Institute of Infectious Diseases
sources.title: Scrub typhus and Japanese spotted fever in Japan, 2006-2009
sources.raw_excerpt: NIID reports Japanese spotted fever surveillance patterns in Japan, tick-bite acquisition, clinical signs, and the need for epidemiological analysis and public information for prevention.
sources.content_text: This reviewed summary reflects the National Institute of Infectious Diseases surveillance review of Japanese spotted fever in Japan. The disease is a representative rickettsiosis caused by Rickettsia japonica and acquired through infected tick bites during outdoor activity. In 2006 through 2009, reported cases increased from 49 to 129 annually, with reporting concentrated in western Pacific-side prefectures and new endemic areas identified. Fever, rash, and eschar are important clinical signs, and severe or fatal cases can occur. NIID states that epidemiological analysis and appropriate information for local people and medical facilities are necessary for infection prevention, prompt treatment, and strengthened surveillance.

content_sections.heading: Epidemiology and clinical features
content_sections.text: Japanese spotted fever reports increased from 49 to 129 annually in Japan from 2006 through 2009, with cases concentrated in western Pacific-side prefectures and new endemic areas identified. Fever, rash, and eschar are important signs, and severe or fatal cases can occur.

content_sections.heading: Transmission and prevention
content_sections.text: Japanese spotted fever is acquired through infected tick bites during outdoor activity. NIID identifies epidemiological analysis and appropriate information for local people and medical facilities as necessary for prevention and timely treatment.

sources.source_name: US CDC
sources.title: About Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE)
sources.raw_excerpt: CDC defines CRE as Enterobacterales resistant to one or more carbapenem antibiotics and describes infection, colonization, transmission, risk groups, prevention, and surveillance.
sources.content_text: The reviewed CDC source summary defines Enterobacterales as bacteria normally found in the human and animal gut that can also cause infections. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales are resistant to one or more carbapenem antibiotics and can include resistant Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Reported clinical syndromes include pneumonia, bloodstream infection, urinary tract infection, wound infection, and meningitis. CRE infection is difficult to treat because of resistance to important antibiotics. People may also carry CRE without symptoms, which is colonization rather than infection. The main described routes of spread are person-to-person contact involving contaminated hands, wounds, or stool and contaminated medical equipment or devices. Patients in healthcare settings have the greatest risk, especially those using ventilators, urinary catheters, or intravenous catheters, those receiving long courses of some antibiotics, and people with weakened immune systems. Risk reduction includes hand hygiene, healthcare patient-safety practices, and using antibiotics exactly as directed. CDC identifies CRE and tracks resistance and healthcare transmission through the Antimicrobial Resistance Laboratory Network, Emerging Infections Program, and National Healthcare Safety Network.

content_sections.heading: Definition and clinical features
content_sections.text: CRE are Enterobacterales resistant to one or more carbapenems. They can cause pneumonia, bloodstream, urinary tract, wound, and meningeal infections; colonization without infection also occurs.

content_sections.heading: Transmission and risk groups
content_sections.text: CRE can spread through contaminated hands, wounds, stool, and medical equipment. Healthcare patients using invasive devices, receiving prolonged antibiotic courses, or living with weakened immunity are at increased risk.

content_sections.heading: Prevention and surveillance
content_sections.text: Hand hygiene, healthcare safety practices, appropriate antibiotic use, laboratory testing, and public-health tracking support prevention and control.

sources.source_name: World Health Organization
sources.title: Guidelines for the prevention and control of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in health care facilities
sources.raw_excerpt: WHO describes carbapenem-resistant gram-negative bacteria as an emerging cause of healthcare-associated infection and provides evidence-based infection-prevention and control recommendations.
sources.content_text: The reviewed WHO source summary describes carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, the name used in the 2017 guideline, as an emerging cause of healthcare-associated infection and a significant public-health threat. These organisms are difficult to treat because of high levels of antimicrobial resistance, are associated with high mortality, and can disseminate resistance through mobile genetic elements. WHO identifies infection prevention and control as a cornerstone of the response to antimicrobial resistance. Its guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for early recognition and for infection-prevention and control practices intended to prevent occurrence and control spread in acute healthcare facilities. The recommendations are designed to support improvement at both healthcare-facility and national levels. This source uses the older taxonomic term Enterobacteriaceae; the surveillance concept in this project uses the current term Enterobacterales while retaining the older label as a search alias.

content_sections.heading: Public-health importance
content_sections.text: Carbapenem-resistant gram-negative bacteria are emerging healthcare-associated pathogens that are difficult to treat and can spread resistance through mobile genetic elements.

content_sections.heading: Prevention and control
content_sections.text: WHO recommends early recognition and evidence-based infection-prevention and control practices in acute healthcare facilities, supported at facility and national levels.
